analogy.p: A rounded number is like a postcode: it tells you which area something is in but not the exact house. The error interval is the whole area that postcode covers, with a boundary on each side. Rounding to the nearest 0.1 divides the number line into neat areas 0.1 wide, and every true value falls into exactly one area. The analogy breaks down because real postcode areas have irregular shapes and edges, whereas error intervals are always exactly one unit wide and sit symmetrically around the rounded value (unless the number is truncated, when the interval starts at the value).
analogy.t: A postcode, not a house number

bullets: A **degree of accuracy** is how precisely a value is given: a number of decimal places, a number of significant figures, or 'to the nearest 10' (or 1, 100, 0.1 and so on).
The **true value** is the exact, unrounded value. The **rounded value** is the approximation we write down.
An **error interval** is the range of true values that could have given the rounded value. It is written as an inequality such as 8.35 ≤ x < 8.45.
The **lower bound** is the smallest true value in the interval. The **upper bound** is the value at the top end of the interval.
Bounds let you decide whether an answer is certain, for example 'both bounds round to 20 so the speed is 20 to 1 s.f.'.
This topic builds directly on rounding to decimal places and significant figures, and on writing inequalities, so check both are secure first.
core.h: Why rounded numbers need error intervals
core.p: Almost every number you meet in real life has been rounded: a length measured as 8.4 cm, a crowd reported as 2400, a speed shown as 20 m/s. A rounded number is **not** an exact value; it is a label for a whole range of true values that would all have been rounded to the same thing. The specification asks you to **use inequality notation to specify simple error intervals due to truncation or rounding**, and (Higher tier) to **apply and interpret limits of accuracy, including upper and lower bounds**. The reason this matters is that every calculation done with rounded numbers inherits their uncertainty, so we need a precise way to say how far wrong the answer could be.

bullets: Step 1: write down the unit of accuracy (the place value of the last digit you are told is correct).
Step 2: halve it. For 1 d.p. half of 0.1 is 0.05; for the nearest 10, half of 10 is 5; for the nearest 1000, half is 500.
Step 3: subtract it from the value for the **lower bound**, and add it for the **upper bound**.
Step 4: write the interval with the lower bound on the left: lower bound ≤ x < upper bound.
Example: 8.4 to 1 d.p. has unit 0.1 and half-unit 0.05, so 8.35 ≤ x < 8.45.
Example: 70 to the nearest 10 has half-unit 5, so 65 ≤ x < 75.
The **maximum possible error** in a rounded value is exactly the half-unit (0.05 in the first example).
Why half? A value of 8.36 is closer to 8.4 than to 8.3, so it rounds to 8.4; a value of 8.34 is closer to 8.3, so it does not. The dividing line is the midpoint, 8.35.
core.p: To find the error interval for a rounded number, first decide on the **unit of accuracy**: the size of the gap between neighbouring rounded values. For 1 decimal place the unit is 0.1, for 2 decimal places 0.01, for the nearest 10 it is 10, and so on. A number rounds to a given value if it lies within **half a unit** either side of it, because beyond that it would be closer to the next rounded value. So the lower bound is the rounded value **minus half a unit** and the upper bound is the rounded value **plus half a unit**.

bullets: The lower bound uses **≤** because the halfway value is included (it rounds up to the given value).
The upper bound uses **<** because the halfway value at the top would round up to the next number, so it is excluded.
On a number line the lower bound is a **closed (filled) circle** and the upper bound is an **open circle**.
Always use a letter in the middle (x, n, l, m) and say what it stands for if the question names it, for example 12.5 ≤ m < 12.6 for a mass m.
Do not write 8.35 - 8.45 or '8.35 to 8.45'; the question says 'inequality notation', so give an inequality.
The upper bound is **8.45**, not 8.4499999. In fact 8.44999... recurring is infinitely close to 8.45, so for calculations we always use 8.45 as the upper bound even though it is not itself attained.
For the answer to be a valid error interval the given rounded value must lie inside it (8.4 is between 8.35 and 8.45), which is a quick check.
core.h: Writing error intervals with inequality notation
core.p: The standard way to write an error interval is a **double inequality** with the variable in the middle: lower bound ≤ x < upper bound. The first sign is 'less than or equal to' and the second is 'strictly less than'. The reason is the rounding convention that values exactly halfway **round up**. So 8.35 itself rounds up to 8.4 and **is** in the interval, whereas 8.45 rounds up to 8.5 and is **not** in the interval. Mark schemes award marks separately for each bound and for the correct inequality signs, so the notation matters.

bullets: 3.7 to 1 d.p.: unit 0.1, half-unit 0.05, interval 3.65 ≤ x < 3.75.
0.46 to 2 d.p.: unit 0.01, half-unit 0.005, interval 0.455 ≤ x < 0.465.
2.0 to 1 d.p.: the zero is a significant, stated digit, so 1.95 ≤ x < 2.05.
0.045 to 2 s.f.: the last significant digit is the 5 in the thousandths, so the unit is 0.001, half-unit 0.0005, interval 0.0445 ≤ x < 0.0455.
2400 to 2 s.f.: the last significant digit is the 4 in the hundreds, so the unit is 100, half-unit 50, interval 2350 ≤ x < 2450.
2400 to 3 s.f.: the last significant digit is the 0 in the tens, so the unit is 10, half-unit 5, interval 2395 ≤ x < 2405.
7000 to 1 s.f.: the unit is 1000, half-unit 500, interval 6500 ≤ x < 7500.
**Check:** an error interval for n significant figures always has a width of exactly one unit (e.g. 2350 to 2450 is a width of 100).
core.h: Error intervals for decimal places and significant figures
core.p: The same half-unit rule works for both decimal places and significant figures; the only skill is finding the correct unit. For decimal places the unit is the place value of the last decimal digit. For significant figures the unit is the place value of the **last significant digit**, which may be in the thousands, the tens, the tenths or even the thousandths. Trailing zeros that are significant (such as the zero in 2.0) matter, because they tell you the accuracy.

bullets: Nearest 10: half-unit 5. Example: 340 gives 335 ≤ x < 345.
Nearest 100: half-unit 50. Example: 1500 gives 1450 ≤ x < 1550.
Nearest 1000: half-unit 500. Example: 62 000 gives 61 500 ≤ x < 62 500.
Nearest million: half-unit 500 000. Example: 3 million gives 2 500 000 ≤ x < 3 500 000.

**Discrete values** (numbers of people, cars, tickets) are whole numbers, so a real count of 'about 2400 to the nearest 100' could be anything from 2350 to 2449. Mark schemes nevertheless normally accept 2350 ≤ n < 2450 and the question will usually say whether to use whole numbers.
**Continuous values** (lengths, masses, times) can take any value in the interval, so the strict inequality with 2450 must be kept.
If a number is given to the nearest 10 and also to the nearest 100, combine the intervals: the true value must satisfy **both**, so take the larger lower bound and the smaller upper bound.
core.h: Error intervals when rounding to the nearest 10, 100, 1000
core.p: When a whole number is rounded 'to the nearest 10', 'to the nearest 100' and so on, the unit is that number and the half-unit is half of it. These questions are very common because they appear in real-life contexts such as attendance figures, populations and distances. A class of 30 to the nearest 10, for example, could really be anything from 25 up to (but not including) 35.

bullets: Truncated to 1 d.p.: unit 0.1, so a value of 5.8 means 5.8 ≤ x < 5.9.
Truncated to the nearest whole number (integer part only): 36 means 36 ≤ x < 37.
Truncated to 2 d.p.: 0.47 means 0.47 ≤ x < 0.48.
Truncated to the nearest 10: 340 means 340 ≤ x < 350.
The **lower bound is the stated value itself** (included, ≤) and the **upper bound is the stated value plus one whole unit** (excluded, <).
Compare: 5.8 **rounded** to 1 d.p. gives 5.75 ≤ x < 5.85, while 5.8 **truncated** gives 5.8 ≤ x < 5.9. The width of both intervals is the same (one unit), but the position is different.
Real examples of truncation: a calculator that cuts off digits, an age (you say you are 15 until your 16th birthday), a price given in whole pounds that ignores pence.
core.p: **Truncation** means cutting a number off after a given place, without rounding. 5.87 truncated to 1 decimal place is 5.8, not 5.9. Because we simply discard the later digits, the true value can be any number from the truncated value up to (but not including) the next value of the same accuracy. So truncation gives an interval that **starts at the stated value** instead of being centred on it, and the whole unit (not half) is added to the top.

bullets: 'Write down the error interval for x' – use the half-unit rule and give lower bound ≤ x < upper bound.
'Give the least and greatest possible values' – the lower bound is the least value; the 'greatest possible value' is the upper bound (accept 8.45 even though strictly it is not reached).
'Could the length be 8.45 cm?' – check the inequality: 8.45 is not less than 8.45, so **no**. 'Could it be 8.35?' – yes, because the lower bound is included.
'A number is 3.4 to 1 d.p. What is the largest it could be to 2 d.p.?' – the true value is below 3.45, so the largest 2 d.p. value is 3.44.
From an interval back to a value: 245 ≤ x < 255 has width 10 and mid-point 250, so it is 250 to the nearest 10.
Where the question says 'to the nearest' always identify the unit before doing anything else. Write it on the page: this earns method marks even when the arithmetic goes wrong.
If the question gives the measurement in different units (for example 1.2 m), keep it in the units given unless told otherwise.
core.p: Examination questions on error intervals come in a few predictable forms and you should recognise each. Sometimes you are given the rounded value and asked for the interval; sometimes you are given the interval and asked what the value was rounded to; and sometimes you must decide whether a particular number could be the original value. In every case, the half-unit rule and the inequality notation do all the work, provided you read what the question says about the accuracy.

bullets: A length 12.3 cm to the nearest millimetre (nearest 0.1 cm) has bounds 12.25 and 12.35 cm.
A mass 4.6 kg to 1 d.p. has bounds 4.55 and 4.65 kg.
A time 24 s to the nearest second has bounds 23.5 and 24.5 s. A time 24.0 s to 1 d.p. has bounds 23.95 and 24.05 s: the extra zero tells you the instrument was more precise.
A temperature 18 °C to the nearest degree has bounds 17.5 and 18.5 °C.
A measurement given to **more** decimal places or significant figures has a **narrower** interval and so is more accurate.
A bound is a **limit**, not a recorded reading: the actual value could be anywhere inside the interval.
The word 'accurate' in the exam usually means 'to the stated degree of accuracy', so state that clearly in answers.
core.p: In science, technology and everyday life, measurements are only as precise as the instrument. A ruler marked in millimetres gives lengths to the nearest millimetre, so a reading of 12.3 cm means a true length between 12.25 cm and 12.35 cm. Limits of accuracy tell you the range within which the true value must lie, and they are the reason the examiner asks about upper and lower bounds. A key idea is that a measurement **always** has an interval, even if the number is written without one.

bullets: Addition a + b: lower bound = LB of a + LB of b; upper bound = UB of a + UB of b.
Multiplication a × b (positive): lower bound = LB of a × LB of b; upper bound = UB of a × UB of b.
Example (area): a rectangle 8.4 cm by 5.2 cm, both to 1 d.p. Lengths between 8.35 and 8.45 and widths between 5.15 and 5.25.
Lower bound of area = 8.35 × 5.15 = 43.0025 cm². Upper bound of area = 8.45 × 5.25 = 44.3625 cm².
Example (perimeter): the same rectangle has perimeter 2(8.4 + 5.2) = 27.2 cm, with lower bound 2(8.35 + 5.15) = 27 cm and upper bound 2(8.45 + 5.25) = 27.4 cm.
Do not round the bounds part-way through. Keep them exact until the end (or show at least 4 significant figures).
Bounds of the final result are always written as exact values from the working, such as 43.0025, not 43.
core.p: When two rounded values are combined in a calculation, the answer can only be as certain as the least certain input. The method is to find the lower and upper bound of each input, then choose the combination of these that gives the **smallest** possible answer (the lower bound of the result) and the **largest** possible answer (the upper bound of the result). For **addition** and **multiplication** of positive numbers this is easy: the smallest answer uses both smallest inputs and the largest answer uses both largest inputs.

bullets: Subtraction a − b: lower bound = LB of a − **UB** of b; upper bound = UB of a − **LB** of b.
Division a ÷ b (positive): lower bound = LB of a ÷ **UB** of b; upper bound = UB of a ÷ **LB** of b.
Example: a = 7.6 and b = 3.2, both to 1 d.p. (7.55 ≤ a < 7.65 and 3.15 ≤ b < 3.25). Lower bound of a − b = 7.55 − 3.25 = 4.30; upper bound = 7.65 − 3.15 = 4.50.
Same example, division: lower bound of a ÷ b = 7.55 ÷ 3.25 = 2.3231 (4 d.p.); upper bound = 7.65 ÷ 3.15 = 2.4286 (4 d.p.).
A sense-check: dividing by a **bigger** number gives a **smaller** answer, which is why the lower bound of the quotient uses the upper bound of the divisor.
Memory tip: for a bound of a − b or a ÷ b, use 'same for the first, opposite for the second'.
For more than two terms, such as a − b + c, apply the rule for each term separately: choose bounds that push the whole expression up (or down).
If numbers can be negative, think about which bound makes the expression biggest or smallest rather than applying the rule blindly.
core.p: With **subtraction** and **division**, using the same bounds for both inputs gives the wrong answer, because the second number works against you. To make a − b as **small** as possible you need a small a and a **large** b; to make it as large as possible you need a large a and a small b. The same reasoning applies to division: to make a ÷ b as small as possible, divide the smallest a by the **largest** b. This swap is the most examined and most commonly mis-applied rule in the whole topic.

bullets: Speed = distance ÷ time. Maximum speed = UB of distance ÷ LB of time. Minimum speed = LB of distance ÷ UB of time.
Density = mass ÷ volume. Maximum density = UB mass ÷ LB volume. Minimum density = LB mass ÷ UB volume.
Area of a circle A = πr² with r = 4.2 cm (1 d.p.): r is between 4.15 and 4.25, so the lower bound is π × 4.15² = 54.11 cm² and the upper bound is π × 4.25² = 56.75 cm² (both 2 d.p.).
Square a **bound**, not the final answer: you must square 4.15 and 4.25, not 'add and subtract an error to 17.64'.
Pythagoras and trigonometry: a hypotenuse c = √(a² + b²) is largest when both a and b are at their upper bounds.
When a formula is rearranged to make something else the subject, redo the reasoning with the new form: it may change which bounds you need.
Write the formula first, then the substitution with the chosen bounds, then the value. Each step can earn a mark.
core.h: Bounds in formulae: squares, areas, speed and density
core.p: Many formulae in the specification combine measured values: area = length × width, speed = distance ÷ time, density = mass ÷ volume, and so on. To find a bound of the result, decide whether each variable should be at its upper or lower bound, according to how it appears in the formula. A variable in the numerator (top) gives the biggest result at its upper bound; a variable in the denominator (bottom) gives the biggest result at its **lower** bound. Squares and cubes of positive quantities follow the order of their inputs.

bullets: Compute the lower and upper bounds of the result (keeping several digits).
Round both to 1 s.f., then 2 s.f., then 3 s.f., and so on. Stop when they first **disagree**.
Report the answer at the last accuracy where they **agree**.
Example: bounds 19.39 and 20.64. To 1 s.f. both give 20, but to 2 s.f. they give 19 and 21. So the answer is **20 to 1 s.f.**
Write a sentence: 'Both bounds round to 20 to 1 s.f., so the speed is 20 m/s to 1 s.f.'. This explanation earns the final mark.
If the bounds do not agree even at 1 s.f., say you cannot give any reliable value to that accuracy; this is rare in exams.
Decimals work the same way: bounds 3.446 and 3.478 round to 3.4 and 3.5 (2 s.f.), so they disagree; to 1 s.f. both give 3, so only 3 (1 s.f.) is certain. Always round each bound carefully.
core.h: Choosing a sensible final answer from the bounds
core.p: Often the final part of a question asks you to **give a value to a suitable degree of accuracy and justify it**. The idea is to compute the upper and lower bounds of the answer, round both to the same number of significant figures, and see whether they agree. The largest number of significant figures for which **both bounds round to the same value** is the degree of accuracy to which you can be certain of the answer. Quoting more than that would claim an accuracy the data cannot support.

bullets: Step 1: list each quantity with its lower and upper bound.
Step 2: write the formula or calculation.
Step 3: for each variable, decide whether the upper or lower bound makes the result as large (or small) as possible.
Step 4: calculate both bounds and keep full precision.
Step 5: answer the question asked: the bounds themselves, one of them, or a rounded value with a justification.
Common contexts: area and perimeter, speed–distance–time, density, unit price, mean of rounded data, similar shapes, and trigonometry in right-angled triangles.
Unit conversions (for example metres to kilometres) should be done on the **bounds**, not before finding them.
If asked 'show that a value cannot be more than…', calculate the upper bound and compare.
core.p: For multi-step bounds questions, a systematic layout is the best protection against errors. Write down all the bounds first, in a small table, then identify which ones to use. Contexts often combine ideas from other topics, so extra care is needed with units and with the order of operations. Remember that the whole point is that **you are not working out one answer; you are working out the largest and smallest answers that are possible**.

bullets: Rounding and significant figures: bounds are the reverse of rounding (given the rounded value, find the true range).
Inequalities: error intervals are double inequalities; they can also be shown on a number line with open and closed circles.
Ratio and proportion: unit price = cost ÷ quantity, so the bounds follow the division rule.
Mean of data given to the nearest whole number: a total of rounded values has bounds, so the mean has bounds too.
Compound measures (speed, density, pressure): the formulae are quotients, so the division rule applies.
Trigonometry and Pythagoras: bounds of side lengths feed into bounds of lengths and angles.
Higher tier extension: find the bounds of expressions such as (a + b) ÷ c or a² − b by identifying which bound of each variable gives the largest and the smallest answer.
Higher tier extension: interpret answers, for example 'the minimum possible area is 43.0025 cm², which is more than 43 cm², so the area is definitely greater than 43 cm²'.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher tier extension
core.p: Error intervals connect rounding, inequalities and the formulae you use in geometry, ratio and science. They also underpin ideas in the real world such as tolerance in engineering: a bolt 12 mm wide will only fit if its true width lies within an acceptable interval. Higher tier questions expect you to carry out the full bounds calculation in unfamiliar contexts and to justify an answer using a statement about bounds.

exam: Command words: 'Write down the error interval' (usually 2 marks: one for each bound, with the correct inequality signs), 'Work out the upper bound / lower bound' (2 to 3 marks), 'Give your answer to a suitable degree of accuracy and justify it' (a final mark for the justification).
A 1 mark question only needs a bound. A 2 mark question needs both bounds with the right inequality signs, or one bound plus a correct calculation.
Always write the half-unit first (e.g. 'half of 0.1 = 0.05'). Even if the final answer is wrong you can still earn a method mark.
Model phrase for the justification: 'Both the upper bound and the lower bound round to 20 to 1 s.f., so the speed is 20 m/s to 1 s.f.'
For 3 and 4 mark bounds questions set out a small table of lower and upper bounds for each variable, then show the calculation using the correct pair of bounds.
Show the calculation with the chosen bounds, such as '485 ÷ 23.5', before writing the answer. A wrong answer with a correct calculation scores method marks.
Quote the bound as an exact or 4 s.f. value in the working and round only in the final answer (if the question allows).
With a number line, use a closed circle for the lower bound and an open circle for the upper bound.
Check by sense: the upper bound must be bigger than the lower bound and the original value must lie between them.
In 6 mark questions that mix bounds with another topic (like area or speed) take the problem in stages, label each line and write the conclusion in context, with units.

mistakes.r: 8.35 ≤ x < 8.45. The lower bound is included because 8.35 rounds up to 8.4; the upper bound is not.
mistakes.w: Error interval for 8.4 (1 d.p.) is 8.35 < x < 8.45 (both strict).

mistakes.r: Add and subtract **half** a unit (0.05), giving 8.35 and 8.45.
mistakes.w: 8.4 to 1 d.p. means 8.3 ≤ x ≤ 8.5 (adding and subtracting the whole unit).

mistakes.r: Use 8.45 as the upper bound. 8.4499... recurring equals 8.45, and the bound is used in calculations.
Lower bound of a − b = LB of a − **UB** of b (the second number must be as big as possible).
mistakes.w: Lower bound of a − b = LB of a − LB of b.

mistakes.r: Lower bound of a ÷ b = LB of a ÷ **UB** of b; dividing by a bigger number gives a smaller answer.
mistakes.w: Lower bound of a ÷ b = LB of a ÷ LB of b.

mistakes.r: The last significant digit is in the hundreds so the unit is 100: 2350 ≤ x < 2450.
Truncated values start at the stated number: 5.8 ≤ x < 5.9.
mistakes.w: Using rounding rules for truncation: 5.8 truncated gives 5.75 ≤ x < 5.85.

mistakes.r: Keep full values in the working and only round at the end, with a statement showing why that accuracy is justified.
mistakes.w: Rounding the bounds early, for example using 43 instead of 43.0025.

mistakes.r: The question asks for inequality notation: write 8.35 ≤ x < 8.45 with a letter in the middle.
mistakes.w: Giving the answer as '8.35 - 8.45' or '8.35 to 8.45'.

summary: You must be able to write error intervals (using inequality notation) for numbers that have been rounded or truncated to a stated degree of accuracy, and, at Higher tier, find upper and lower bounds of calculations with rounded values (add, subtract, multiply, divide, formulae) and give a justified final answer. It matters because every real measurement is only approximate, and examiners reward a precise, notation-correct description of that uncertainty.

terms.d: How precisely a number is given, for example to the nearest 10, to 2 decimal places or to 3 significant figures.
Replacing a number by a nearby simpler value at a stated degree of accuracy; values exactly halfway round up.
Cutting off a number after a stated place without rounding, so the digits after that place are simply discarded.
The range of values that a rounded or truncated number could have been, written using inequality notation.
The smallest value in an error interval; it is included in the interval (≤) when the number was rounded.
The value at the top of an error interval; for rounding it is the halfway value above, which is not itself included (<) but is used in calculations.
The place value of the last digit given, such as 0.1 for 1 decimal place or 100 for the nearest 100.
Half the unit of accuracy; it is subtracted from the rounded value to get the lower bound and added to get the upper bound.
The greatest amount by which a rounded value can differ from the true value; it equals the half-unit.
Writing a range using signs such as ≤ and <, for example 8.35 ≤ x < 8.45.
Data that can only take separate values, usually whole numbers such as the number of people.
Data that can take any value in a range, such as a length, mass or time.
The digits of a number that carry meaning about its size, counting from the first non-zero digit.
The upper and lower bounds within which a measured or calculated value must lie.
A measure made from two others, such as speed (distance ÷ time) or density (mass ÷ volume).

worked.q: (a) a = 3.7 correct to 1 d.p. (b) b = 2400 correct to 2 s.f. (c) c = 5.8 truncated to 1 d.p. Write down an error interval for each. [3 marks]
steps: (b) The last significant digit is the 4 in the hundreds, so the unit is 100 and the half-unit is 50: 2400 − 50 = 2350 and 2400 + 50 = 2450.
(c) Truncation: the interval starts at 5.8 and goes up one whole unit (0.1) to 5.9.

worked.q: p = 7.6 and q = 3.2, both correct to 1 decimal place. (a) Find the upper bound of p − q. (b) Find the lower bound of p ÷ q, to 4 s.f. [4 marks]
steps: (a) Upper bound of p − q uses the biggest p and the smallest q: 7.65 − 3.15 = 4.5.
(b) Lower bound of p ÷ q uses the smallest p and the biggest q: 7.55 ÷ 3.25 = 2.32307...

worked.ans: Speed = 20 m/s to 1 s.f., because both bounds (20.64 and 19.39) round to 20 to 1 s.f.
worked.q: A runner covers 480 m (to the nearest 10 m) in 24 s (to the nearest second). Calculate the speed to a suitable degree of accuracy and justify your answer. [5 marks]
steps: To 1 s.f.: 20.638... → 20 and 19.387... → 20. To 2 s.f. they would be 21 and 19, which do not agree.
So the speed is certain to 1 s.f. only.
